speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion implies complete endorsement of a draft bill which the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) laid on the table with the report. I was a member of this committee although for some time I was ill and unable to attend. I must say that I heartily commend not only the legal talent but the judicial attitude taken by the hon. member for Swift Current as chairman of this committee. But this report deals with certain fundamentals which, if accepted, I think would be prejudicial to the conduct of the democratic representative system which now prevails in this country
3868	COMMONS
Electoral Matters-Special Committee
Heretofore the Dominion Elections Act provided penalties for all corrupt acts which influenced or tended to influence the votes of electors, but candidates and their official agents were free to incur expenses in good faith for all purposes which were not deemed and declared by the Dominion Elections Act to be corrupt.
For example, expenses incurred in good faith to secure a proper revision of the voters' list in order to eliminate from the voters' list the names of those who were not duly qualified electors and to prevent illegal voting have always been a legitimate expense. Again, expenses incurred in good faith for necessary professional services actually performed for the purpose of preventing the illegal registration of voters and illegal voting and to secure the proper conduct of an election have always been deemed to be a legitimate expense. Again, expenses incurred for the fair cost of printing and advertising and for stenographic services and postage for communicating with and instructing electors, have always been deemed a legitimate expense. Again, expenses of public meetings at which addresses may be delivered to electors, including the hiring of halls and meeting places, advertising meetings and the expenses of broadcasting political addresses have up to the present time, always been regarded as a legitimate expense.
These and similar expenses were deemed to be not only legal but necessary for ensuring freedom of discussion which is the fundamental basis of democratic representative government. This form of government is possible only when free public discussion of public questions is not only permitted but encouraged so that the electors may be fully informed in relation to the political issues, upon which the verdict of the electors is sought when an appeal is made to the electors of the whole country or to the electors of any electoral district.
The Dominion Elections Act of 1938 was enacted after being reviewed by this same committee on electoral matters. Section 65 of that act, after defining in nine clauses every form of corrupt practice, states:
Provided always that the terms of this section shall not extend or be construed to extend to any money paid or agreed to be paid for or on account of any expenses legally payable and bona fide incurred at or concerning any election, and provided that the actual personal expenses of any candidate and his expenses for professional services actually performed and for the fair cost of printing and advertising and for halls or rooms for the holding of meetings shall be held to be expenses legally payable.
That is the law at the present time. You will note particularly, Mr. Speaker, that any expenses legally payable and bona fide incur-[Mr. Cahan.J
red at or concerning any election, including personal expenses of a candidate and his expenses for professional services actually performed, the fair cost of printing and advertising and for halls and rooms for the holding of meetings, are now declared to be expenses legally payable.
In addition to that, a candidate's personal expenses are defined by the act of 1938 in section 2, subsection 25, as follows:
(25) "personal expenses" as used herein with respect to the expenditure of any candidate in relation to the election at which he is a candidate, includes the reasonable travelling expenses of such candidate and the reasonable expenses of his living at hotels or elsewhere for the purposes of and in i elation to such election, and all other expenses which, except as restrained by this act, he may in person lawfully incur and pay.
The words "except as restrained by this act" refer to provisions which compel the candidate to have certain election expenses paid by his official agent.
This proposed bill by clause 22 of section 62 as drafted provides:
(22) With the exception of personal expenses lawfully incurred by a candidate, no election expense shall be incurred or authorized by a candidate or by his official agent in respect of any candidature as a member to serve in the House of Commons of Canada in excess of a sum equal to twenty cents for each name on the official list of electors for the electoral district for the current election.
On ten different occasions I have been a candidate at dominion or provincial elections; two of those were federal elections for rural districts and two of the provincial elections were for rural districts, and my personal expenses in either of those four elections in rural districts never exceeded $1,000. The expenses in a rural constituency are postage, travelling about the constituency, and the hiring of halls. I do not know what the practice is now in rural constituencies, but I never was called upon to pay more than five or ten dollars for a hall or meeting place for one night in country districts-sufficient to pay the janitor's services and the light. In the country districts they were always glad to make either the school house or the community hall available for discussion. But in a city constituency it is very different indeed. I am not criticizing any party, I am not criticizing any person, and I trust that anything I may say will not be regarded as a reflection upon particular individuals.
I am dealing now with the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George in the city of Montreal.. I should think that probably St. Lawrence-St. George has a larger number of alien residents than almost any other district

Electoral Matters-Special Committee
in the island of Montreal or the province of Quebec. It is a great commercial centre; citizens of the United States and their families are resident there, and citizens of other foreign countries are engaged in commercial enterprises in the constituency. A very considerable number of aliens reside there who have never become naturalized Canadians.
My experience is that the present method of preparing the lists, by sending out enumerators who are engaged not for their knowledge of the law or their proficiency in deciding issues of naturalization and nationality, results in about four to five thousand names being returned by them of citizens who are not qualified to vote, either by nationality at birth, or by naturalization. So far as I am concerned I would not object very much to allowing these names to remain on the electoral list, because the majority of them or a great number of them are of reputable persons who would not attempt to vote at an election at which they know they are not qualified to vote. But leaving their names on the list, and assuming that they do not vote at the election, provides facilities for a crime to be perpetrated which is probably not peculiar to my constituency but certainly prevails there to a very considerable extent, the crime of impersonation. Leaving the names on the list allows those who engage in impersonation and in illegal voting of that description to appear at the polls and vote in the names of those who they know will not attend at the polls to vote.
But that is not the whole story. They attend and vote in the names of those properly qualified to vote, and in some cases the impersonation of women voters is the worst of the lot. I have known cases where eminent ladies in St. Lawrence-St. George have been impersonated by women gotten up to represent them, who appear at the polls early in the morning, and when the qualified electors appear they find that someone has voted in their name. Of course, the qualified elector may take the proper oath of identity and still vote, but women cannot often be prevailed upon to do that. Many business men coming to the poll and finding that others have voted in their names are so disgusted that they turn away and say, "If that is the way elections are conducted, I will have nothing to do with them."
I intend to give an illustration. Part of my constituency is a provincial constituency known as the St. Lawrence division. The provincial election of 1931 was held on August 24, 1931. The result of the vote appears in public documents which I have here, published by the officers of the provincial government. I wish
to note a few of the remarkable results achieved by the impersonators.
No. 48 was a polling subdivision with two polling stations. The station which contained names from A to L had 91 names on the list, and it was a closed list; no names could be added on election day, as is possible in the rural districts. With 91 names on the list, 96 polled their votes. In the station from L to Z, with 78 names on the list, 112 votes were polled. So that, taking the whole of polling division 48, with 169 names on a closed list 208 votes were polled.
In No. 69 there were two polling booths In one, from letter A to N, 81 names were on the list and 100 votes were polled; in the other, from O to Z, 52 names were on the list and 68 votes were polled. So that foi the whole polling division, with 133 names on the list, 168 votes were polled.
In No. 70 there were two booths. In the one with names from A to L there were <2 on the list and 75 votes polled; in the other, from M to Z, with 61 on the list, 62 votes were polled.
Or take No. 71, with two booths. In the one with names under letters A to M there were 70 on the list and 91 votes polled; from N to Z there were 68 on the list and 100 votes polled. So that in that polling division there were 138 names on the list and 191 votes polled.
In polling division 72 there were 99 names from A to K on the list and 121 votes polled; from L to Z there were 101 names on the list and 120 votes polled: in all, in that division there were 200 names on the list and 241 votes polled.
In No. 73, from A to L there were 105 on the list and 111 votes polled; from M ta Z. 96 on the list and 105 votes polled. So that in polling division 73, 201 were on the list and 216 votes polled.

I will keep the house for
only a few moments. I am trying in restrained language to present the case which actually occurs. Now why should I not be allowed to hold public meetings, and as many, in my constituency as I deem necessary? I have no public hall in my constituency except halls which are attached to one or more of the churches. There is one-I do not know whether it is in my constituency, if not, it used to be when my constituency included a part of the ward of St. Louis; I refer to the Prince Arthur street hall where in the attic the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and labour unions and some others occasionally meet. But it is in an attic, and difficult of access, and women are afraid of it as a fire trap. For me to hold a public meeting in my constituency costs on an average at least S500. I have to hire one or more of the large dining rooms of the leading hotels, at a cost, if I remember correctly, of about $200. If I advertise that meeting in the city press, it costs at least $150 for advertising. If I have any broadcasting, it costs $150 more- in all, about $500 for a public meeting with a local broadcast so that all my constituents may hear me. Why should I not be allowed to make that expenditure? Why should I be put on the same plane as the candidate in a country constituency where such expenditures are not necessary except on a very moderate basis?
Therefore what I say now is that I shall vote against the motion of the hon. member for Swift Current, because to vote for that motion to my mind carries with it an approval of all that the bill attached to his report contains. And that bill must be read in conjunction with the main act as passed last session. I have stated the reasons why I cannot vote for it, why I must oppose it. When the bill comes before the house it must, I assume, be introduced by a member of the government. I trust that the government, before they approve the bill and introduce it as a government measure, will carefully consider the criticism which I have made and decide whether there may not be some amelioration of the distressing circumstances and conditions to which I have called attention. Personally I wish to impose no expenditure

upon any candidate. Any candidate is free not to make any such expenditures, but I am bound, if I am to prevent criminal practices in my constituency, to take measures to prevent such impersonation and fraud; I intend to do it to the extent that I may do so legally, and I do not think this parliament should preclude me from so doing.
I should like to suggest an amendment. I am simply going to read it now, to show the line along which I think the government should consider an amendment of this bill. It is a mere suggestion, not a motion. It is that clause 22 of section 62 be amended to read as follows:
22. With the exception of personal expenses lawfully incurred by a candidate during an election to an aggregate amount not exceeding one thousand dollars, and with the further exception of expenses incurred bona fide by or on behalf of an official agent, during or in connection with an election, in the preparation and revision of the list of electors and in preventing illegal voting, expenses for professional services actually performed, expenses for the fair cost of printing and advertising and for halls or rooms for the holding of meetings, and expenses for broadcasting political addresses by or on behalf of a candidate during an election, no election expense shall be incurred or authorized by a candidate or by his official agent, in respect of any candidature as a member to serve in the House of Commons of Canada, in excess of a sum equal to . . . cents for each name on the official list of electors for the electoral district for the current election.
What I wish is to restore in principle the exception made in the present existing act of 1938 whereby all these expenditures were declared to be legal unless it was clearly shown that they were made for corrupt or illegal purposes.
This motion to accept the report cannot pass except on a division, and if it shall pass on division I shall make no further objection now. Having stated my case to the government, I trust that before the bill is introduced its members will take into consideration the matters to which I have called attention.
Hon, C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):	May I join
with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) in expressing the appreciation of, I am sure, all hon. members of the work carried on by the members of the electoral committee during the past four sessions. I do not know of any committee of this house that has laboured so long and so carefully in dealing with the various matters confided to it for consideration. The members of this committee have dealt with most complicated questions, matters which have been in controversy over a long period

Electoral Matters-Special Committee
of years, such as the alternative vote, proportional representation and compulsory registration and voting, and have made reports to this house which I believe will be studied and consulted for many years to come. After a careful study of all existing legislation, both in Canada and in other parts of the empire, the committee brought in last year an election act which in the opinion of, I believe, the vast majority of the members of this house is as complete an act as it would be possible to place on the statute book under any circumstances.
Our thanks, I think, are particularly due- and in this I join with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George-to the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell). The work of a committee such as his involved the exercise of discretion, judgment, tact and diplomacy, all of which are possessed by the hon. member for Swift Current to a degree not surpassed by any hon. member of this house.
I think I should also say a word, in which I am sure hon. members in all parts of the house will concur, in regard to the counsel to the committee, Mr. Harry Butcher, a former colleague of ours. Mr. Butcher has devoted a great deal of time and energy to the study of these questions; and by way of digression, so far as my experience goes he is the only individual ever to be permitted to address secret caucuses of all the political parties represented in this house. Mr. Butcher, I understand, was allowed to give an explanation of the 1938 election act to the caucus of each political party in this chamber. I think that speaks well for him, and perhaps indicates that sometimes at least members of this house are not unduly imbued with the partisan spirit.
With respect to this suggested legislation, in some respects at least I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. The proposals do not meet with all the requirements I might have considered essential. The proposed bill perhaps may not be as radical as the measure which was presented to this house a year ago. In connection with some matters the recommendations are perhaps not sufficiently restrictive in the way of expenditure. But I suggest that the two main principles contained in this proposed legislation should commend themselves to the members of the house. The first is the limitation of the expenditure permitted by a candidate. The second is something new in our legislation, a recognition of the fact that in addition to the candidates in any given constituency there are certain organizations which have a vast influence in the issue of an election, namely, large political organizations;
and that those political organizations, in order to function, must have campaign funds. The country and parliament will at last recognize the legal existence of something at the very name of which we have hitherto shuddered. It is proposed by the committee in this legislation that we recognize campaign funds, that we regulate them and publicize them so that every person in the country may know the sources from which these funds come.
With respect to the first principle, dealing with the limitation of expenditure on the part of any candidate, almost every country in the world has some such provision in its election legislation. Great Britain has it; the United States has it; Ireland has it; Australia has it; New Zealand has it, and as far as I am aware many of the countries of Europe have it also. In many countries the limit is far lower than that proposed in this legislation. We have, I think, come to the almost unanimous conclusion that it is not right or fair that the wealth of a candidate should be a material factor in his election as a representative of the people. Ever since the franchise has been granted, ever since man has had the right to exercise the franchise, it has been restricted by extraneous factors of one kind or another. In the early days, as the house well knows, the right to vote was strictly limited to the propertied classes. Later there was intimidation of the voters by these same propertied classes, and in many instances an election was a foregone conclusion because the tenants were obliged, either by custom, by practice or by coercion, to vote for their landlords. Still later we ran into the question of undue influence, industrial, clerical and governmental; and now, in our modern days, we come across something which is almost a greater obstacle to the free choice of the people than any I have enumerated, namely the power of money. Given an election in which there is no very great public issue clearly defined, wherein the public are apt to be confused by the slogans of the various parties; given to any candidate the right to use unlimited money for propaganda, for the hiring of halls, for the employment of the genius of the modern advertising man and the pushful tactics of the modern high pressure salesman, all the eloquence of paid orators on the radio, a wealthy man is an extremely difficult man to defeat in a constituency, however just the cause of the other candidate may be. Therefore, I say there is justification for the limitation of expenditures in a constituency.

I am coming to that point. I am free to admit that the point raised by my hon. friend is a serious one. As yet I have not considered it, but I propose to deal with it in a moment. I am not aware as to whether the committee considered that matter. It strikes me that there would appear to be quite an anomaly at first sight in suggesting a limitation in a constituency and having none in connection with the national organization. Before leaving the matter of the local organization, I might suggest that to allow unlimited expenditures in a constituency, as is the case now, is unfair to the constituency and detrimental to the general interests of the country.
Then, with respect to campaign funds of a general party organization, I do not believe there is any question which has more thoroughly aroused public opinion in this country-over a long period of time, particularly in recent years, than the matter of campaign funds. But I believe public opinion has been unduly aroused; I am convinced that the immense campaign funds which are mentioned on all and sundry occasions exist only in the imaginations of those who mention them. Any-one who has been as close to political organization work as I have knows that there is nothing harder to get than campaign funds when they are most urgently required. But the opinion does exist that there are such funds. Whether or not that opinion is well founded, it is deeply implanted in the minds of a large majority of our people.
There is the further thought that these funds are used corruptly, however much they may be used legally. There is also the thought that those who subscribe are doing something detrimental to the public interest and harmful to the country as a whole. My hon. friend, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), the former leader of the opposition, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and many prominent men have expressed the view in this house-I am not giving their exact words-that a man has as much right to subscribe to his political party fund as he has to subscribe to his church or to any other organization. In that view I heartily concur. But the public has a right to know where these funds come from. The public has a right to be able to trace the sources of the funds by- which propaganda is carried on behalf of a political party. Whether these subscriptions be large or small, there should be something on our statute books to force those who feel inclined to subscribe to have their names known to the public. I do not think I need labour this point any further. The matter has been discussed time and again
[Mr. Calian.l
and I think the people generally of this country approve of publicity being given to campaign funds.
That this publicity will dry up some of the sources of these funds, I do not deny, as I have stated already, but- I do believe that as long as these funds are hidden, as long as the exact size of funds is not known, then those who attach themselves to political parties, those who like elections in order that they may benefit in their own pockets, will be constantly pulling at the purse-strings of the various parties because of the belief that the funds are unlimited. The moment the amount of these funds is known to the public it will be possible to tell the hangers-on that they cannot get that which they desire. In other words, if we have less money, we will squander less.
Speaking purely from the standpoint of one who has taken part in elections and election organization, I believe what we need most in this country is the education of our people to the fact that campaign funds cannot be picked off trees, that it is a delusion to imagine that because a general election is on, millionaires will empty their pockets on behalf of one political party or another, and that all one has to do is to make the suggestion to a political party in order to have it indulge in the wildest form of extravagance; that things which would not be done in private business will be done because it is in the alleged interests of the party. We should educate our people, and we shall be obliged to educate them, to the belief that civic spirit, interest in their country, interest in their own particular locality and their own selves will do more for the good of the country than the expenditure of thousands on publicity and similar activities. We must tell them that if they staunchly and firmly believe in the political party which they support, they will support that party because of their principles and in order to put the party into power. If that is done I think they will soon come to the conclusion that there will be no reward at the end other than the ordinary reward of virtue.
A word with respect to the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. On many occasions my hon. friend has explained to this house the particular difficulties which exist in his constituency.
I do not think any member of this house, least of all myself, would contradict him in any way. If he believes that the state of disorder which he describes constantly exists, we have to take his word for it. But I fail to follow his argument when he states that because

Electoral Matters-Special Committee
there are among his electors, or among those who reside in his constituency, people who would take advantage of the law7 to perjure themselves or to commit criminal acts, this parliament should authorize the expenditure of money to an extent to permit him to set up a private army of his own to control this lawlessness. I took it from his observations this morning that he proposed to engage his own private constables. He complained of political patronage in the state engaging one constable, but with all my respect and even veneration for my hon. friend he would hardly be likely to make the general of his private army a member of another political party.

speechtext: I shall not ask my hon. friend to apologize. I have never in twenty-five years in parliament risen to a question of privilege to call anyone to order, but I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to give me the same show, if I need it later in this discussion, that is given to every member. If this is going to be a private fight, let it be so. I say that my hon. friend introduced a bill the object of which was to change the decision of a judge, the chief justice, no less, of the superior court of the province of Quebec, Chief Justice Greenshields, his decision being that no one who was already on the electoral list could have his or her name struck off without due lawful proof being given that they had no right to vote. I have here the decision of the judge. My hon. friend's private army, after the enumeration had been made by the official enumerators, one from each political party, as provided for then and as is provided for now, checked over that list and decided that of about twenty-five or probably thirty thousand odd names on the list of electors in my hon. friend's constituency, five thousand were illegally on the list, and my hon. friend's friends proceeded to make affidavits that these persons had no right to vote. The registrar declared in fact that these electors' names should be taken off the list. The electors, as is the right of every citizen of Canada, and as is provided for by the act, appealed to the judge of the superior court of the province of Quebec.

He was appointed by the dominion franchise commissioner. I have here the judgment of Chief Justice Green-shields. I have not the date of it, but it is signed by "R. A. E. Greenshields, J.C.S." I do not want to go through all the particulars, but in deciding what evidence should be required by the registrar before striking a name off the list, my own conclusion after reading the judgment was that the evidence which the registrar had accepted was hardly sufficient and that, unless proper evidence was given to the contrary, these people's names should remain on the list. It was to reverse a decision of the learned judge in that court that my hon. friend asked for legislation by this house. Apparently there were only two hundred cases that came before Judge Greenshields. His judgment was read into the records of this house on June 21, 1935, by you, Mr. Speaker, when in happier times you were sitting on the other side of the house. The affidavits to disfranchise these various people appear to have been made by a gentleman named Prowse. In his judgment the chief justice says:
It may be here stated that after the notice of appeal was served on the registrar, the objector, Prowse, desisted from his objection and purported to desist from the order given by the registrar striking the names of twenty-three out of the two hundred.
So that as soon as the appeal was made, this private investigator decided that he would not like it pressed to the point where evidence would be taken, and so he desisted.
Quoting further from the judgment:
I now deal with the proceedings before the registrar, on the twenty-second of May, as disclosed before me. In the first place Prowse was the objector in all the two hundred cases. From his own testimony it appears that he did not know, personally, one of the two hundred against whom he made an objection. In the second place, he never saw one of these electors against whom he made these objections. What he did appears by his testimony. He went to the residence, as shown on the official voters' list. In some cases he found a vacant house, or a house into which he could not obtain entrance. How long that house had been vacant he has no idea. He therefore asked somebody for information, and somebody, whom he had never seen before, and whom he does not know, informed him, that the house was vacant; that the former tenant had moved away. subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Euler for the second reading of Bill No. 63, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
When the house adjourned last night I was on the point of offering some criticism of the bill now under discussion. I believe that 70 cents is altogether too small a price and that we ought really not to consider so low a figure. The lowest price that we should even give any consideration to is 80 cents a bushel, basis Fort William. We really ought to restore the 87i cents which was decided upon in the past, and we should take such steps as will enable us to offer men $1 a bushel at the earliest possible moment. To some people that will seem an extreme request, but I feel certain that the months which are ahead, and the years, will prove that that request is not exorbitant. We may find to our sorrow that we have gone too far in letting the farmers of western Canada suffer under too low prices. I believe also that it was a very unwise move on the part of this government to allow to fall into disuse the

Canadian Wheat Board

advisory committee consisting of seven members, including at least four representing farmers.
The farming industry surely deserves to be given more consideration than we are giving it. According to figures which I have, during the last sixty-two years the farmers of western Canada have raised 8-9 billion bushels of wheat, worth 10-2 billions of dollars, of which 6-1 billion bushels have been exported, bringing to this country 7-2 billions of dollars. What the west has been able to do it may do again if given a chance. It may do even better than that; for by the use of the projects which the Minister of Agriculture is so wisely undertaking in western Canada under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the west can greatly increase its productive capacity of almost any kind of agricultural commodity.
In discussing the question of the deserts of the west, may I repeat in passing that according to Doctor Jacob Viner in his testimony before the Rowell commission in March, 1938, the three prairie provinces of Canada have been contributing 847,000,000 a year under the tariff to the support of the Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: How much have the other provinces contributed?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Well, that is not the matter we are discussing at the present time.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: It is important.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: They are getting the benefit.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: The reason I mention this, as I pointed out yesterday so many times, is that hon. members rise in this house and imply that when we give western Canada a few million dollars we are giving them a gift-they are "milking the east," and that sort of thing. Certain people, such as the premier of Ontario, seem to be obsessed with the idea that the west is milking the east. That gentleman needs to inform himself.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: That is the prairie provinces, or does it include British Columbia?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Just the prairie provinces. Now, $47,000,000 does not sound very much until you multiply it by 10 for ten years, and by 20 for twenty years.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: And how much for a hundred years?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
When they remember the few dollars contributed by this government to support the west, hon. members will see that there remains still a great deal of latitude for generosity towards the west.

So much having been said, I turn to the question of costs, which has been very much dealt with in the committee. Upon this subject I think I can probably suggest one or two ideas which have not yet been authorized.
The average cost of producing wheat after summer fallow on eight experimental farms during the years 1923 to 1930 was 817.40. The average yield was 27-4 bushels; the cost per bushel therefore 64 cents. I submit that if the experimental farms, conducted under the dominion government, with all the equipment and advantage from the possession of the most modern devices, found that it cost them 64 cents a bushel, that should give us reason for serious pause when we remember that tens of thousands of our western farmers are struggling under genuine adversity which results in their being unable to use to greatest advantage their means for producing wheat. It is well known that it takes money to make money. If a man has to produce without money it surely increases his costs, and the suffering for him is much greater-at least that is likely.
The highest yield and the lowest cost per bushel on any of the experimental farms during the period 1923 to 1930 occurred at Lethbridge, my own central city, in 1928, when 52 T bushels per acre were produced at a total cost of $18.32 per acre, or 35 cents a bushel. The lowest yield during that period and the highest cost was at Scott, in 1924, when 7 bushels per acre were produced at a cost of $14.08 per acre, bringing the cost per bushel to $2.01.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Does not that show the difficulty of placing costs upon a bushelage basis?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Exactly; I do not question that for a moment. But it also shows the variability of income to which the western fanner must of necessity be subjected.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: For one year.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

We must bear in mind that a man may start well off this year, and, because of the variability of his income, the vicissitudes through which he must pass, find himself bankrupt in ten years. As far as Canada is concerned that man's solvency at the end of ten years is of as vital concern as his solvency to-day. Any long-range policy must take into consideration this variability factor.

I quote from a publication entitled Cost of Producing Farm Crops in the Prairie Provinces, by E. S. Hopkins, J. M. Armstrong and H. D. Mitchell, division of field husbandry, dominion experimental farms, bulletin No. 159, new series, published in 1932. The total cost per acre, as I have said, was $15.70; the yield in bushels was 30-8, and the cost per bushel 51 cents for that period. To be perfectly honest we must admit that costs were a bit inflated during the roaring twenties; but when we single out such an item as manual labour and find that it is allowed only 25 cents an hour and horse labour only 8 cents an hour, I think we must grant that sufficient moderation has been exercised in computing costs. In addition to the 51 cents we have the hauling to the elevator, which is not counted, and also the freight to Fort William, at least 18 cents a bushel, plus the handling charges.
That presents a serious picture. We must bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of this country are producing their crops under a very wide variety of circumstances. Many have farms remote from elevators; some are ten, fifteen, twenty and twenty-five miles away. If they are to succeed, some allowance must be made, in striking an average, for the mishaps of the man who is twenty miles from an elevator, and who probably has to pull up hill and down dale.
I turn now to another aspect of the question. The yields are very variable. The yields at Lethbridge, between 1912 and 1930, were as follows:

I point to the yield of 2-2 bushels per acre in 1919 and ask the house to reflect on that for a moment. I was farming there at that time. The blow our establishment received was so great that we were staggering for years in an effort to recover our loss. We lost not only on our crop but also on our live stock and every other aspect of farming. There were scores of families around us not so fortunately situated and perhaps in an even less favourable position to recover than we were. Many of these farmers simply passed out of solvency forever as a result of their operations during that one year.
The figures I have quoted represent more or less ideal conditions. Anyone who has been around an experimental farm knows that conditions there are far better than the conditions which ordinarily surround the average farmer who is trying to raise a family and meeting with a variety of mishaps. Here are some considerations which must be borne in mind. Many of our farms, and this is particularly true of Alberta, contain hilly land. It costs more to farm hillsides than to farm level areas, and often we have to farm small patches of a hillside. I grant that you cannot make allowance for all these things, but if we are to safeguard the stability of our farmers throughout the country we must remember that many of them are on farms where conditions are not by any means ideal, where all the land1 is not cultivable or equally easy to work. There are some valleys on our farms; sloughs occupy a share of many of the farms throughout Alberta and Saskatchewan. We have low lands, which are bad lands because of the alkali they contain. We have sandy stretches, which are unprofitable. Two or three hon. members have already mentioned that a good many of our farms are homesteads. I have had a kindly feeling towards the minister because several times already he has indicated that he has homesteads in mind. Do we want homesteads on which men live and raise families? I think it will be agreed that we do. Very well, then; we must adapt our behaviour to meet the situation confronting the home-
Canadian Wheat Board

steaders, who suffer many mishaps-frost, insects, droughts, large and small, hail, winds, soil drifting, and so on. How many times in actual practice have we who live on the farm lost a very fine crop just because of an inopportune rain lodging heavy grain.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when
the house took recess I was discussing the various elements which help to make the farmer's life very uncertain and his income extremely variable. I had mentioned frost, drought, hail and wind, and now I wish to refer to the cost of irrigation. A great many irrigation districts are being developed, and the idea is that as soon as a man is on an irrigation project his problem is solved. That is not so, by any means. Frequently he has added to his other troubles the cost of irrigation. There is, first, the capital charge and, second, the service charge from year to year. The result is that even in irrigation districts a farmer has to be constantly looking after the costs of production. Where wheat is being raised on such a project, there is still another element involved.
Debt for the average farmer is completely inevitable. A great many people imagine that the farmers get into debt through carelessness, but it should be remembered that in order to establish a farm, a farmer must go into debt for his land and equipment. When such a farmer must face variability of income, the growth of his debt is unavoidable.
There is another matter which is becoming quite serious, at least in two of the western provinces, and probably in the three. Not so many years ago when I was a boy we looked upon wheat as being more or less a side line. We were able to make our living from dairying and by raising a few sheep and hogs as well as carrying on a number of other activities. Even potatoes were a source of income upon which we could regularly depend. Because of the conditions which have arisen, largely since the war, to-day hardly any one of these different products will yield the farmer an income. For a number of years beef has been sold at below cost in my constituency. Almost all other meats, with the possible exception of pork, are in the same class. Milk and milk products are almost hopeless as a source of income, and vegetables and potatoes have long since ceased to be profitable except for those few who have special markets in the cities. Fruits

are in the same class. Wool is so variable in price that frequently the producer is not able to count on a profit on his year's work. Prices are ruinously low and destructively changeable. Under these conditions I think we can say with positive assurance that Professor E. C. Hope, who has been quoted many times already, is on sound ground when he says, as reported on page 152 of the proceedings of the conference on markets for western farm products:
Conservatively it would probably require with average yields a farm price for wheat of average grade of about 90 cents, with coarse grains in proportion to maintain a reasonable level of living and service the present debt on western farms. It would require somewhat more than this to restore the farming community to the condition of 1931.
In the light of these words I contend that when I ask that wre have at least 80 cents, that the price of 87^ cents be restored at an early day and that we may look forward to a price of SI per bushel at no distant time, I am asking nothing more than the situation requires.
There is another matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister in the light of what I have said already. The government cut the price of wheat 7} cents in August; this bill cuts it another 10 cents, which in effect means that the price of wheat to the western farmer has been cut 17i cents in one crop year. Had the 87} cent price been a generous price, this cut would have been serious, but the 87i cent price was just a barely tolerable price. There was no greater need to cut that price this year than there was in 1935. The farmer's need is just as great to-day as it was in 1935, and the government's need is no greater because revenues are just as buoyant to-day as they were in 1935. I can see no reason for this betrayal of the farmers by the government.
The advisory committee was abolished, which took from the farmers the right to have a say w'ith regard to prices, which right they felt was theirs. Then these grievous cuts have been made. The government has given the farmer a shabby deal.
I had occasion yesterday to refer to the place from which the money would come. Speaking from a purely orthodox point of view I wish to remind hon. members that we in western Canada are making our full share of contribution to the revenues of this country. I have referred to the $47,000,000 which is a net contribution over and above the protection we receive. When I recall the sales tax which we pay, the income tax, excise tax, and the full share of other taxes which we pay, I am sure I am correct in saying that the

Canadian Wheat Board
west is contributing to this government, over and above the services which it derives therefrom, to an extent sufficient to justify the government in treating the western farmer generously.
I mentioned yesterday what other countries are doing for their farmers. I believe every civilized country is helping its sugar beet industry. For example, the United States is making substantial contributions to the beet sugar industry, as are Britain, France and Germany. What is Canada doing?

I appreciate the ideas of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I realize his point of view, but I think he also realizes mine. More will be said on that later.
In this parliament and outside a great many people have raised this question: If you guarantee a higher price for wheat, you will induce an overproduction of wheat which will

Let me examine that argument. The member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) rather threw out a challenge to all members of the house, and I think he had us social crediters particularly in mind. Let me mention a few things, for the benefit of the hon. member for Rosthern and other members of (the house, which this party would do with respect to any surplus of wheat that would result from giving a reasonable price. But first let me point out that in order to avoid an overproduction of wheat this government is starving the industry down. Instead of so managing matters that the people can consume the production of the industry, they are endeavouring to hamstring and smother the industry, which is exactly the wrong way of going about it.
There are several things with respect to surpluses which would develop in any country like Canada, equipped and endowed as she is, if you gave a reasonable price to the producers. In the first place you must enable the people of Canada to consume what they need of all agricultural products, such as sugar, meats, dairy products, poultry, honey, wool, furs, canned goods. Some people will say that is not good sense. Let all those who are inclined to that view consider tlhe words of Sir John Boyd Orr, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen, in a dispatch from Montreal, dated May 5, 1939. I think his opinion is worthy of respect.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Who is he?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
I am surprised that there should be members who do not know that Sir John Boyd Orr is one of the outstanding nutrition experts in Great Britain. He has this to say:
England's nutrition problem may be a vital one but that of Canada is even more vital. The danger is recognized in England and legislation to counteract it is in force.
The implication is that the danger is not recognized in Canada, and I believe that Sir John Boyd Orr is correct in his statement. He said further:
By far the majority of your lower wage class, those earning $1,500 and less, live on a diet inadequate for health.
The dispatch goes on:
Sir John advocated "a national food policy designed to make a diet fully adequate for health within the purchasing power of every class, even the poorest. . . .
What is lacking here is regulation of the food standard. This nutrition committee is full [Mr. Blackmore.l
of the latest scientific knowledge in this connection, and is filled with enthusiasm to get that knowledge put into application."
Sir John outlined such schemes as issuing vouchers to needy persons with which they could obtain food at greatly reduced prices.
"And here is the whole point. The supplying of food to the poor, or rather putting it in their reach, is directly the route to economic prosperity. For, if the large masses of underfed start eating more and better foods, the present surplus of farm products would be removed, agriculture would boom and with it economic stability would return."
Whether his words are worthy of consideration or not is one matter. But there can be no doubt that the ill which he points out and the remedy he suggests are worthy of consideration.
First of all, stimulate consumption in this country to the extent to which people can use all the agricultural products they need. Then we shall find that several things will begin to happen. Take sugar, for example. In my province we can very soon be equipped to produce fifty per cent of the sugar consumed in this country. Think of how many thousands of acres would be taken out of wheat production by that means.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

But then the hon. gentleman was a little cautious. He said, "I grant that you cannot make allowance for all these things." He admitted that, and I praise him for his reasonableness.

Oh, yes, my hon. friend was sincere when he said that you could not do it, that it was not feasible. But I will continue. Then he came back to his old mania and quoted some other things. There are the hillsides. But why forget those who live in valleys? Fourth on the list is the valleys. "Sloughs occupy a large area on many of the farms throughout Alberta and Saskatchewan." So those who are on the hillsides and those who live in the valleys must have a contribution from the state. But there are not only valleys, there are low lands "which are bad lands because of the alkali they contain." And that is not all. There are "sandy stretches too which are unprofitable."
All this is from the geographical point of view. But there are many other reasons why the farmers should be indemnified. Said he, "We must adapt our behaviour to meet the situation confronting the homesteaders, who suffer many mishaps." So we must consider the homesteader who is on the prairie, who is on the hillside, or in the lowlands, or in the valley. And for these reasons: first, frost; second, insects; third, droughts, large and small; fourth, hail; five, winds; six, soil drifting and so on; and seventh-and here comes something which is pleasant for many farmers-the rain. Just a minute, Mr. Speaker. "How many times in actual practice have we who live on the farm lost a very fine crop just because of an inopportune rain." There must be an insurance against rain. Why should there not be insurance for sunshine also? Note that the hon. gentleman says,

Canadian Wheat Board
"We who live on the farm." What does the Parliamentary Guide, which contains the hon. member's autobiography, say about this "living on the farm"? I find in the 1939 edition, page 138:
A school teacher. Member of Raymond school board 1916-17; Alberta Teachers Alliance; Alberta Social Credit League.
And he says, "We who live on the farm"!

Were it not for the tariff we should have our sugar by the bag from Cuba and the West Indies, and the electors of my hon. friend's constituency would not be able to grow sugar beets. He says that we should produce fifty per cent of our sugar. Well, there is nothing that is impossible to my hon. friends in that group. Why do they not change the climate of the country and produce sugar cane? Someone says "Hear, hear." The one who says that is a chef and he is accustomed to making good things. Of course he might like to change the climate, and I hope that if he does he will pay attention only to summer diet.
Then the hon. member for Lethbridge, who by the way is the leader of his group, says that if you guarantee a high price for wheat you will have a surplus that you cannot dispose of. At any rate this authority is a distinguished Englishman who gave some lessons about what should be done in this country. But may I point out that conditions in England are entirely different from those in Canada, because England is not a producing but a consuming country; and those who follow the newspapers know that England greatly fears famine in time of war for the simple reason that the farmers do not produce enough for the needs of the country. I could give a long lecture to the hon. gentleman on the way in which the farmers are treated in Great Britain, but I have not the time to-day. Perhaps- next session, if we have an election and if he is elected, I shall have something to say to him. There can be no possible comparison between Great Britain and Canada, because, as I say, Great Britain is a consuming and not a producing country, whereas Canada is both.
The hon. gentleman speaks of stimulating consumption, and he talks about fifty per cent of sugar by tariff. Does he know that the money which the people of the prairie provinces receive comes from the taxes paid by the people of Canada in the form of customs and excise and sales taxes, et cetera? I may tell him, moreover, that if the taxes are not reduced but continue to be a burden upon the Canadian people it is because of the extravagance of members of his group, who are asking for more and more. I am sure that if it had not been for this question of wheat-I am expressing my own opinion, without any official information-the budget this year would have been entirely different and we would have had some relief from taxation. Stimulation of consumption and fifty per cent of sugar by tariff! And yet he complains of taxation. Then he suggests carpenter work and talks about surplus in store. They had kept a lot of wheat in storage and refused to sell, expecting better prices. And what happened? It is useless to deny that there was exploitation on the part of westerners in connection with sales of wheat in England during and after the war. At that time they were taking advantage of the British market in this way, that they thought the British people would never be able to secure wheat from other sources than Canada, which was supposed to be the granary of the world. They were holding on to their wheat, allowing the British people to go hungry because they could not afford to pay $3 and more per bushel, and the price declined. Why? Because the British people, who have a real business sense, thought of investing in other countries in order to get cheaper wheat. That was done particularly in the Argentine, where British capital was invested in the growing of wheat. That was one reason-there was in the Argentine another source of supply for England. Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members in this house will agree that it is indeed delightful to listen to the wise words of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), particularly when he is speaking on behalf of the eastern division of the Liberal government of this country. Apparently there must be two divisions of the Liberal party, the western and eastern divisions, and they do not seem to belong to the same caucus. I can find no other explanation of the widespread disagreement between the views of the hon. member for Temiscouata, who speaks for the eastern division, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who might be said to represent the western division of the Liberal party in Canada. Just a moment or two ago the hon. member for Temiscouata told us that Canada had been spending hundreds of millions of dollars in order to support the western farmers; yet only two or three days ago the Minister

Canadian Wheat Board
of Agriculture said ia this house that up to 1935 wheat had not cost this country a single cent. That makes me wonder whether these two gentlemen belong to the same caucus. I do not believe they do. Apparently there must be a wide divergence of opinion within the ranks of the Liberal party; and when the eastern and western divisions cannot agree they look up the Conservative platform and endeavour to use that as a basis of agreement.
I cannot possibly let it be said that we in this group do not truly represent the people of western Canada. Personally I believe my people have been in this country at least as long as those of the hon. member for Temiscouata. My family were pioneers in this country; we have lived here a great many years. My point is this: I know definitely that we are in close contact with the people of the west. Some of us are not farmers, but we belong to that complex economic system which goes to make up the life of every individual in the west. We are well aware of the problems of the people of western Canada, simply because every single thing that affects them affects us, no matter if we are school teachers or if we follow other professions. We are closely related to our people; their problems are our own.
I listened carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata, and I think the greatest truth he uttered was his statement that the difference between Canada and Great Britain is that Great Britain is a consuming country and we are not. How true those words are! England is a consuming country; we are not. I know he is correct because across this country there are thousands of young people with hardly anything to eat, which proves the statement of the hon. member that they are not consumers. Even in his own constituency, where he says the people might not listen to us, I am sure there are some people who do not get as much western wheat as they could use.
There was also a statement made concerning the effect of the pool policy of 1929. I can find no better way to answer this argument than to quote from the submissions by the wheat pool organizations of western Canada to the royal grain inquiry commission when it sat at Calgary and Regina in April and May, 1932. The following statement is made about the pool policy of 1929:
My attention has been drawn to comment in Canada upon a statement made by me in the House of Commons on the first of April. The suggestion that the statement was based upon any feeling that the pool had been attempting to hold up wheat is wholly baseless. My statement was made in reply to an opposition supplementary question and was based on
assurances given me, by you, at Winnipeg, in September, that the pool had been anxious to sell at prices substantially lower than those prevailing. I fully accepted these assurances, and welcomed them as evidence of a friendly attitude towards my plans for encouraging more regular interchange of goods between Canada and Great Britain. I trust you will give full publicity to this explanation. As you know, I fully appreciate the difficulties with which the pool has been confronted, and I earnestly hope the situation may soon rectify itself to the advantage of both countries.

I come from the Peace River country, in the northern part of Alberta, the district possibly the farthest removed from railway outlets, the district which

Canadian Wheat Board
pays a higher freight rate upon grain than any other part of Canada. Any variation in the price of grain or in the conditions affecting the marketing of it is bound to affect our part of the country more than any other, simply because we are so far removed from markets. When a price of 70 cents a bushel is fixed, past experience leads us to believe that it will be the maximum price, and if that be so, a greater injustice will be done to the people of the Peace River country than to the farmers of any other part of Canada because of the great distance we are from our markets.
I do not wish to speak at further length at this stage but shall reserve my questions until the bill is in committee. But I could not let it be said that we who live in western Canada do not truly represent the people of that part of the country. I extend to the hon. member for Temiscouata an invitation to visit the Peace River country and see for himself what we have there. He will find settled there many of his compatriots who,
I am sure, will give him a welcome, and give him too what he does not believe in, a lesson in unity. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has people living out there and has done us the honour to pay us a visit; so we do not expect to hear him using the language of the hon. member for Temiscouata. In order to have unity in Canada we must take a broad view of our problems. We in this group are willing to do so, and when we rise in this house to speak we do so from a sense of responsibility to those who have sent us here, and for no other reason. I am sure all other hon. members do exactly the same. But let not the fact that we are not all farmers, that some of us may be school teachers, take away one ounce of weight from the arguments we present. We present them knowing thoroughly the conditions of the people of our constituencies. We are for the most part farmers and are pleading for the farmers of our constituencies. It is our duty to do so and we shall continue to do so, whether or not our speeches are burdensome to some hon. members. They may not like them, but we must make them listen because that is the only way we can get justice in a democracy.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have retained my seat for a number of days and listened with close attention to the discussion pro and con in regard to these very important, indeed vital, measures proposed by the government to deal with what all thoughtful men and women in this country recognize to be a serious economic situation. I deplore the spirit of antagonism
which seems to have obtruded itself into the discussion. Parliament, as I understand it, is a great forum, the most important in Canada, where the elected representatives of the people are supposed to approach the different questions that come before them with a degree of sanity and calmness, and may I add intelligence, that will enable this forum ultimately to find solutions for the various problems presented. The one now before us is perhaps the most important and in some respects the most tragic problem that has been presented to parliament for consideration, with the possible exception of the great problem of unemployment, which also has engaged our attention.
As a matter of fact, there ought to be no conflict between western Canada and eastern Canada.
I look upon the two great divisions of this country, industrial eastern Canada, and western Canada, largely agricultural, as complementary one to the other. Sitting here I have wondered if we have in mind at all the anxiety and the strivings of Hitler, as the leader of industrial Germany, to secure for his great country some of the productive wheat plains of the Ukraine, Hungary and other parts of central Europe. He looks upon those wheat plains as necessary to the economic life of his country, and to secure them, where he has not actually taken them over as he did Czechoslovakia, he strives to bring them into intimate commercial relationship with Germany. In Canada we have the industrial east and we have the great plains of the west. One is complementary to the other: Instead of raising every possible point of difference in our economic relations, let us pause for a moment and see if there are not some grounds of common interest.
It is true that the west has been a most valuable market for eastern Canada's manufactured goods, for its implements, clothing, furniture, kitchen utensils and other products. On the other hand, I would ask my friends from the west to keep this in mind: Not only do the largely populated centres of eastern Canada constitute a valuable market as consumers of western wheat; they are also large consumers of live stock, hogs and cattle, which are constantly flowing in trainloads from the west to the eastern markets of Toronto and Montreal. So the east is an exteremely valuable market for the products of the west. In recent years there has been an increase in the production of butter in western Canada, particularly in Manitoba and Alberta, and this product also finds a valuable market in the industrial sections of the east. So we have
Canadian Wheat Board

this situation in Canada: a growing industrial area in the east which is complementary to the primary production of the west, and vice versa.
Let me say, in justification of my taking part in this debate, that I have lived in the west for forty-five years. I have watched those plains develop. There are not many in the house-I know there are a few-who have been longer in western Canada than I have. But I have .been there long enough to watch its development, from the days when the jack rabbits and antelopes ran rampant over the plains, until to-day when we see that vast agricultural area for the most part under intense cultivation.
Let me make one further reference, inspired by some of the observations made by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). When I first went west the movement of people to that country came preponderantly from Ontario, Quebec and the eastern provinces, but from Ontario perhaps more than from any other part of Canada. Scarcely a train moved westward without a car of what we used to call settlers' effects, containing a few horses, some implements, some feed, and the usual utensils, with a son of some farmer in the east proceeding to the west to settle on a homestead.
Then came the great movement from Europe and from the United States. One of the problems with which we as a parliament are confronted arises from the fact that a substantial proportion of the settlers on the western plain are not of original eastern stock.
I believe that the foundation stock was, but the subsequent migrations, particularly from the central western United States and from Europe, constitute a large proportion of the population, and they are not acquainted in any considerable detail with the history and the background of eastern Canada.
I should like to utter, if I may, just a word of caution and advice to some of my western friends. There is [DOT] a danger in overstating a case. There is a danger, in our anxiety to put forward the point of view of those in whom we are interested and whom we represent, of so strongly emphasizing it that it is overstated and reacts against the cause we are seeking to espouse. On the other hand, I believe I am equally justified in saying to some of our eastern friends who perhaps have not gone west and have no personal knowledge of its problems and difficulties, that it will not do to look upon the west as a sort of poor relation. Both attitudes are entirely wrong. We should be mighty proud of this country we call Canada, proud of the magnificent development of the west

and the sacrifices of the early settlers. Goodness knows they had to make sacrifices; they suffered hardships far beyond what are suffered to-day, because there was no outside help; they were on their own resources, and there was very little in the way of communication. Only one railway track, the main line of the Canadian Pacific, stretched across the plains. On the first trip I made west there were no such things as air brakes; I do not believe there was a sleeping car; certainly there was no dining car. When one considers the progress and development of the last thirty to fifty years one cannot but be impressed by the fact that those who went into the west in the earlier days were pioneers deserving of our recognition, our commendation, and our support.
Having said that, I should like to come to the measures before us. Let me say to the ministers concerned that while I see merit in these bills-in the one which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) is now sponsoring, and in the rehabilitation measure which preceded it-it must not be assumed that by passing them we shall have solved the problems confronting western Canada. These are but palliatives, temporary measures to meet a condition which must be frankly recognized. There are some parts of these measures of which I do not approve, but it must be admitted that they make some contribution to the solution of the problem.
The real problem, stated very briefly, is twofold. There is the question of market dislocation, and there is the other question, physical and natural, of drought plus exhaustion of the soil. I am under the impression that up to the present time successive ministers of agriculture have not attached sufficient importance to the contributions which that department might make to solving these difficulties. Time will not permit me to analyse them in detail. But let me say a word or two about markets.
I believe that there are two approaches to this question. One is an improvement of internal consumption. This opens up a wide vista. To my hon. friends who have been occupying a good deal of the time in the debate on this question I would say that merely railing against the tariff of this country will make no contribution to the extension of Canada's home market. I am not going to digress into a long discussion on that, but let me remind some hon. gentlemen opposite that from 1911 to 1914, when we of the Conservative party sat on their side of the house and the Liberals occupied the seats on this side, the Liberal representatives from the west;, led by the veteran Hon. Frank Oliver of

Canadian Wheat Board
Edmonton, used almost the identical arguments which my hon. friends have been using here for the last four or five days, objecting, as they used to express it then, to the growth of "trusts, mergers and combines." Those words were flung across the floor of the house, and the discussions took very similar lines to those of the present day; but very little good came of it all. There is a possibility, and it ought to 'be substantial, of greatly extending the consumption of agricultural products in Canada through a wise and judicious application of industrial protection; because this country, with its tremendous power resources, is peculiarly adapted to an increase of the industrial population, and as that population increases there will be an increase of the home market consumption of farm products.
The other method which I suggest and which has been mentioned is one with which I shall deal but briefly, namely, the intensification of our effort to secure new outlets. What has happened in recent years to restrict the available external market, for wheat in particular, is beyond our control. Let us understand that very clearly. We must,, however;, suffer the effects of it. And while I refer to intensified efforts to secure external markets, I am aware that we are seriously handicapped because of world conditions and factors to which I have alluded but upon which I shall not enlarge.
Let me say a word with regard to natural difficulties and troubles. In my opinion no policy to deal with this western problem will be complete unless it takes into consideration the whole theme and policy of conservation. I believe that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), in particular, as well as the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and my venerable friend from Melville (Mr. Motherwell) will bear me out when I say that during the last forty years or more, through the draining of sloughs and by one process and another, there has been, over the plains, a lowering of what is called the water table, with the result that the subsoil moisture there has largely disappeared. Then, following the dry weather and an almost total absence of rain, we have the dried out area and the dust problem. These are not peculiar to Canada. All we have to do is turn our eyes southward and we find that Kansas, Arkansas, Montana, Idaho, the Dakotas and other states down to the Mexican border have passed through a similar experience.
Let me say this-and it is applicable both to the United States and to Canada. I believe that we have been remiss in our duty as nations in not long ago recognizing that
in regard to the drought problem there were factors which were purely human and which we should have taken steps long since to remedy. I suggest that the whole question of conservation should challenge our attention, and the same is true of the questions of the restoration of fertility of soil by the use of proper fertilizers, the water problem, which is being touched upon by the minister in one of his bills, and kindred questions.
I might submit this thought to the minister. The Department of Agriculture is equipped to carry out great public works, and what we have done this session is to erect a second public works department within the Department of Agriculture. In my opinion, we are going to have a very unsatisfactory experience, because amateurs are being given the task of constructing extensive water conservation projects, which should be taken charge of in a large national way and be placed under the control of the most expert and most experienced engineers the government can find. There is no doubt in my mind that a proper study of the various watersheds of western Canada would reveal that, by diversion, conservation and so on, we can bring back to the arid areas of that part of Canada a large supply of water.
Then there is the question of farm methods, and again I say to the Minister of Agriculture: Here is a realm which, while not altogether neglected, is certainly not dealt with by the Department of Agriculture as it should be. For instance, recently we have had laid before us the activities of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, indicating that they have gone into an intensive study of the derelict farmers whose loans became past due and were taken over by the company. Last year-and the hon. member for Temis-couata might well be reminded in this regard that because a person is not a farmer he is not always foolish-that great company alone restored the condition of economic security and self-sufficiency to 2,700 farms in the United States. That is not very large, but that was one company acting on its own. Here is a great field in respect of which the Department of Agriculture could take advantage of the opportunity presented to them.
Another thought is this, that we ought to take a long view of the problem. It is no use coming here this year and declaring, as we have done in the other bill, that this year will be considered an emergency year. This is the month of May and we do not know what will happen. It is an admission that we do not know what to do, but we are presenting these bills and will declare this year to be an emergency year in any
Canadian Wheat Board

case, so that whatever happens we shall be more or less prepared, to the extent of these measures, to meet the emergency. That is not taking the long view. We ought to think of this problem in terms of generations. What is fifty years? I do not want to appear old, but I must say that, looking back, fifty years seems like yesterday. The forty-five years that I have been in the west is in reality a short period of time; but looking ahead, forty-five years seems interminable. I submit, however, that in this whole problem we ought to be looking at the question in terms not of to-day or of to-morrow or of next year, but of the generations to come.
One further reference to this measure before us. It is a sort of revamping of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and I am not going to criticize seriously the minister's set-up. I will say this, however. At the present time an intelligent survey of the world situation would, in my opinion, indicate that there may be an increase in the market value of wheat during this year. We are fixing the price at 70 cents- " a sum certain " is the term used. That is nothing more or less than fixing the price. It is an initial price. We are fixing the value at 70 cents, Fort William basis. Now that goes out to the world as a declaration from Canada that this is the measure of Canada's value of wheat. I do not care whether we intend it or not, but that is the impression that is being conveyed. Canada, having led in the export of wheat for so many decades, is naturally looked upon as giving the lead.
I submit, therefore, that we should have done one of two things. Either we should have left the fixation of price open as before, and then the price could be fixed in the light of conditions that might obtain, we will say, in July or thereabouts, or we should have fixed the price at 80 cents. I am not saying that it would have been wise to fix a price of 80 cents instead of 70 at this time. I should have preferred to see the price left open as previously, and then, upon conference with the producers and the trade, and taking all factors into consideration, a fair price could be fixed for the initial payment in the month of July, say. That was preferable to the present situation.
