It was not my intention to go into a lot of detailed discussion, but I repeat that it would have been better to leave the price open as in the original bill, and to fix it at the opportune time rather than fix a low price such as 70 cents, or 60 cents as originally suggested. Also I think that the arbitrary limitation of 5,000 bushels cannot in its very nature work out fairly or equitably. I am not going to make any detailed analysis of the matter, but I think in principle it is wrong. It might be

I do not know-that a
few large producers would benefit unduly. If so, some exception could be made to cover them. But a farmer such as was mentioned by the chairman of the agriculture committee last night, who works quite an area with a good-sized family in the expectation of having these sons take part of his farm later on- and I understand there are many such-would be unfairly penalized by this provision. This is only an illustration of how an arbitrary cut-off at 5,000 bushels will work injustice. It may be a sort of compromise with those who object to the whole scheme, but such a compromise usually has more or less danger in it. I object to that feature.
I do not intend to delay the house. My real purpose in rising was to point out two things, mainly. One is that these measures are not a satisfactory solution of this economic problem which is facing the country, of which we ought to take a long-time view. We should deal with it not only as it affects us to-day, but from the point of view of remedies which will affect the situation in the next generation as well. The other is, as I said in my opening remarks, that this country is really not divided into two economic sections. If we persist in that view we shall inevitably come to the disintegration of confederation. There is no other end. You cannot go on, particularly in this forum, quarrelling about the detailed economic problems of one section as against another, without coming to separation. To persist in such a course is unnecessary; it is not true; it is not right. We have a great country; one section is complementary to the other, and if we approach these questions from the point of view of the value of one section to the other, seeing how by working together we can make the most of that advantageous position, then we can make some headway.
I have one other suggestion, and it is particularly applicable to the present situation. Let us not forget that our one great export market for wheat is Great Britain. Virtually not a bushel finds a market south of the line; yet I call hon. members to witness that during this whole session the trend of the argument bearing upon economic life in Canada has been-and this comes from those who are most vociferous in their protestations on the wheat problem-that our economic future is more tied up with the United States than with Great Britain and the British empire. Just as the east and the west of Canada are complementary to each other, so in the export realm the British empire, and particularly Great Britain, is complementary to Canada.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much of the time of the house, but I think some things should be said which so far have not been said. Yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) took the position that each of these bills was separate and should be discussed separately. I take the position that these bills are complementary to each other, that they cannot be divorced from each other and, therefore, must be considered together in order that we may get the whole picture.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is to be congratulated upon the fact that the policy of an acreage bonus has been adopted by the house. That is something I did not expect to see accomplished so soon. I believe this is the first legislative attempt made by any government to frame an agricultural policy which would affect the whole of Canada, not only the west but also the east. If this does something to allay that spirit of disunity which has been made manifest even to-day in this house, I think the minister is entitled to credit for that, at all events.
I must confess that when this policy was first introduced I had grave doubts as to its value. I believe at that time my thoughts were directed more to the fixed price or initial payment, as it is called, than to the other part of the program. I realize that no farmer seeds his land in the expectation of a crop failure; he looks forward to a crop which will return him a certain amount of money, and the thought in my mind in the first instance was that the farmer would be able to look only to the 60 cents as the basis of that return. I also know that this figure of 60 cents could not begin to compensate the farmer for his work and the costs he incurred in connection with his crop. I knew that this figure would create a certain amount of opposition, and I think we all agree that the opposition has been considerable. Naturally I, together with other western members, made strenuous representations to members of the cabinet as to our point of view with regard to these proposals; and, together with other western members, I take some credit for the increase from 60 to 70 cents, although

Canadian Wheat Board
at the same time there was a reduction in the acreage bonus from fifteen to twelve bushels to the acre.
Just here may I refer to some remarks, made in a rather sneering manner, in regard to the efforts of the western members. Some speakers have endeavoured to say that the members of the cabinet had a pistol pointed at their heads by members from western Canada, and that in consequence they had to change their policy. I should like to know whether, in connection with a project such as this, we should not represent the viewpoint of the western members; and I should like to know why, as private members, we are not entitled to give to our cabinet, within our own party, the point of view we hold, in order that they may bring in legislation we think suitable to our country. That is what we did. It is no secret that we camped on the doorsteps of the ministers for days and weeks, until the legislation was brought down. That it is entirely satisfactory none of us will say; but that it has a considerable degree of sufficiency I think most of us on this side of the house will agree.
Some changes have been made in the bills as originally brought down, but I say unhesitatingly that the policy of the Minister of Agriculture has not changed in the slightest. We still have a wheat board, which has always been requested by the west. We still have an initial payment, which has been increased from 60 to 70 cents. We still have participation certificates, by which farmers who sell to the board are entitled to reap any profit that may be secured in the sale of that wheat; and we still have the acreage bonus, reduced from fifteen to twelve bushels to the acre. In addition, we have had a further amendment which affects Manitoba. Our representations were that the figure of 135 townships was too large, and the minister has seen fit to bring down that figure, so far as Manitoba is concerned, to 100 townships, or a little better than eleven municipalities. That is something for which we thank the minister, because we believe that in Manitoba 100 townships is a much more equitable figure than the original proposal.

Some hon. members have
indicated that their point of view is being regulated by conditions in their constituencies. I do not consider that the comprehensive viewpoint to take, but I do not think they can quarrel with me if I take my own constituency as a basis for my supporting the government as I intend to do on these bills.
In 1937 when I went back to Marquette I found that all the territory west of the Assiniboine river right up to the Saskatchewan boundary was in exactly the same condition in regard to drought as the territory just on the other side of the line in the constituency of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). But my constituents in Marquette were not receiving any relief as were the constituents of my hon. friend from Melville, and I had of course to make what representations I could to the government. I came to Ottawa to see the Minister of Agriculture in order to ascertain what could be done to help them. He was in the position that the law did not permit him to help them, and therefore he could not accord any relief to my constituents. And I had the spectacle of men taking hay from a reserve east of my home town and going into Langenburg in the constituency of Melville because on that side of the line the people were getting all kinds of relief while my people were getting none. I say to those who speak with regard to their own constituencies that in my constituency, if this acreage bonus had been in effect, our farmers would not have had to endure all the hardships and troubles which they have experienced.
In some parts of my constituency the initial payment will be the feature upon which the farmers will focus their minds, but in other parts of the constituency it will be the acreage bonus. I recall a man who had nothing from his farm last year, not even feed for his horses, and he had difficulty in getting food for himself. He did not want to go on relief and he said, "If the municipality will only pay for feed for my horses I will go on the road and work it out." But the municipality could not do it. They could only give him relief in the form of food for himself and his family. As a consequence the province came into the picture and provided the relief which these people required.
As I said, I at first focused my mind on the initial payment, but the more I considered the acreage bonus I realized that in it we had the foundation of a policy upon which we could build, so that western Canada might some day look forward to the time when they can look after their own troubles, and I know of no other policy, Mr. Speaker, that is likely to lead to that rarilt.
I realize, of course, that the fixed price in 1938, without the acreage bonus, was abso-

lutely inequitable. One of the large farmers of my district said to me, "I am in favour of the 80 cents, of course, because I have a large crop, and I get a good deal of government money, but a man on the other side of the road has no 2rop and it is absolutely unfair that I should receive the 80 cents and he get nothing and have to take relief." That is how it worked out. So, when I began to consider this whole proposition afresh, while I should have liked to see the 80 cent price, or more if necessary, I am of opinion that the 70 cent price which the government has already fixed, together with the acreage bonus, enables me to go home and offer something to my people. Those who have crops get a secured price. It may come about, as some hon. members have suggested, that the initial payment will, in such instances, not mean anything. Nevertheless the farmers will have an opportunity of selling to the board and receiving a secured price of 70 cents, together with participation certificates which will enable them to share in any profit which may be made on the sale of their grain.
I think, therefore, the proposition as we have it to-day is a reasonable one, and one that will be accepted by the people. I am fortified in that view because when I went home at Easter there was in my home town a large and representative meeting of the farmers of the whole surrounding district. They were there concerned only as to a fixed price of SO cents. We discussed the whole question, and the result was that the meeting, which was one representative of the whole countryside, including part of the drought area, passed a resolution that the initial payment of 70 cents, together with the acreage bonus as then proposed by the Minister of Agriculture, was satisfactory.
In the following week I took the opinion of the members of my executive, a large number of whom were present. We discussed the whole matter pro and con. They realized what the acreage bonus meant and also the value of an initial payment of a large amount, and with one exception, all the members of the executive were of opinion that in the circumstances of to-day an initial payment of 70 cents with the acreage bonus would be satisfactory to western Canada. They were looking, not to the men who had a large crop and therefore were obtaining money, but to those who might have no crop and who would in those circumstances get some benefit from the acreage bonus plan proposed by the Minister of Agriculture. The executive did mention at that meeting that hail should be included, but the Minister has already explained to the house why hail is not included.

In the acceptation of these bills by western Canada I should state at once that we are not bargaining with eastern Canada or any other part of Canada; we are not saying that we are receiving protection for our products in western Canada; we are not giving eastern or any other part of Canada an opportunity to say that we in the west have now accepted the doctrine of protection. I cannot reconcile indirect taxation with its benefits to industry, with a direct, specific and known amount paid to the wheat growers. If the government paid a specific and known amount to industry, in the form of wages, say, there might be a parallel with this initial price. But the tariff granted to an industry is to protect the home market of that industry. It has its effect on the industry by largely excluding competition.

This section 2 contains the phrase, " to buy and sell wheat." The board will be obligated to sell wheat, and in view of the situation that we face I was wondering if the government had any plan whereby our sales of wheat might be increased. This bill is in charge of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). I have before

Canadian Wheat Board
me Hansard of March 14, 1929, and on page 948 I find that a former Minister of Trade and Commerce, Hon. Mr. Malcolm, gave as his opinion at that time that the Department of Trade and Commerce was not exercised over the sale of such commodities as wheat, because these commodities find their own markets. Those are the words of a former Minister of Trade and Commerce, and consequently I think the particular phraseology of this bill is of importance to us at the present time. This afternoon we heard it alleged, and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) said that he agreed, that much of our difficulty had been caused by the holding policy of the western pools. We have a wheat board now, and if accumulations occur they cannot be attributed to the former policies of any cooperative organization. I should like to point out that I disagree with the statement to which I have referred, and I think the records show that it is incorrect. I do not propose to go into the records to-night, but I have them before me on my desk. Suffice it to say that the case for the western producers was stated very well in the submission made to. the royal grain inquiry commission which sat in Calgary and Regina in 1937.
Therefore I ask the minister what special efforts the government proposes to make in view of what is going on in the world. According to press reports, the United States is endeavouring to exchange wheat for other commodities and to subsidize the export of wheat. Just before I came into the chamber this evening, I heard part of a news dispatch in which it was stated that the announcement had been made to-day in the British House of Commons that an agreement had been entered into between Great Britain and Roumania, and one of the products that Great Britain had undertaken to receive from Roumania was wheat. I did not hear the quantity. In view of the methods adopted by the United States and other countries, in view of the treaties that have been entered into by other nations with our best customer, I was wondering if the government has any policy, not only to buy but to sell wheat.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

I think I can assure the committee that the government and the wheat board are constantly concerned with selling as much wheat as possible. In fact, in the trade agreements which we have made, consideration is given to wheat. I might mention Germany which has been obliged to allot a certain amount of exchange for the purchase of wheat. In other negotiations which we have carried on, wheat has never
been lost sight of, and that commodity will continue to receive every possible attention.
Reference has been made to the British market. It is well known that this is our largest market for wheat, and I think it is sure to remain so. The wheat board has been quite active in carrying on an advertising campaign in an effort to induce bakers and the public generally to consume greater quantities of Canadian wheat or Canadian wheat flour. The wheat board has a man abroad constantly, a Mr. Biddulph, whose sole work is to promote the sale and consumption of Canadian wheat. I believe they have even gone to the extent of making motion pictures, one being called "The Kinsman." Possibly my hon. friend has seen it. The board has spent a good deal of money in advertising and, as I say, it employs this one qualified man who is mostly in Great Britain promoting the sale of Canadian wheat.
Reference has been made to articles in the press to the effect that the United States is negotiating some sort of barter arrangement by which it will exchange something like
100,000,000 bushels of wheat for, I believe, rubber and tin. In reply to inquiry, I informed the house some days ago that the government of Canada is cognizant of the situation, and that we had communicated through our high commissioner in London with regard to the matter. No definite reply has yet been received, but the government is not at all blind to this situation and is giving attention to the matter.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

speechtext:
I have in my hand a
copy of Hansard of July 4, 1935, containing a debate which bears directly on the question raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. So far as Roumania and the United States are concerned, and Roumania in particular, Great Britain has always bought part of her wheat supplies from Roumania, and in view of the circumstances existing in Europe to-day Great Britain would hardly discontinue purchasing wheat from Roumania, preference or no preference. There is a situation existing in Europe to-day in relation to Roumania which makes it natural that Britain would be making deals in wheat with her, but probably in no greater quantities than she has taken annually over a long period of years. Speaking in this house on July 4, 1935, the then Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett, made quite plain the position under the wheat board act in relation to the buying and selling of wheat. At page 4271 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
We return now to the next item, the duties of the board. The board is to be prepared at all times to buy wheat and pay for it a fixed

Canadian Wheat Board
price. That fixed price having been determined and the board having paid it, as it will be obliged to do under this bill, it then must consider the next point. How would it be sold? The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth and those associated with him kept pressing the point with respect to sales, and there was introduced into this bill-I got their notes and tried to give effect to their view-the provision that the board should sell its wheat at such price as might be considered reasonable with the object of promoting the sale and use of Canadian wheat in world markets.
In other words, there was not to be a holding policy. He goes on:
That is the principle that governed Mr. McFarland's operations in every particular. The board must regard as reasonable the price at which it sells. Then we come to the next point, which is that it should take over, secondly, the wheat of the Canadian wheat producers; and I pointed out this evening in answer to a question asked that the present thought in our minds was that you would substitute the board for Canadian Cooperative Producers Limited with respect to wheat and wheat only.
Then he goes on at page 4272 of Hansard:
Now the question is, how shall the accumulations be disposed of? That is the next question. This year's crop is to be dealt with in the way I have indicated. The accumulations, which came about in the way I have indicated, are to be dealt with as provided in the act in a special section, namely by their disposition as speedily as may be reasonably possible having regard to economic and other conditions. In other words, the accumulations are not to come into competition with the crop produced this year. As speedily as may be reasonably possible having regard to economic and other conditions -there are the conditions that you have with respect to the sale of the accumulations, and above and beyond all that-and the suggestion in a slightly different form came from the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-there is paragraph (h):
To give effect to any order in council that
may be passed with respect to its operations.
That is, the governor in council has the power of directing, prohibiting, controlling, regulating, determining the course of action this board shall take with respect to any matter that comes within its jurisdiction.
I wanted to read that because of some comments made on both sides of the house in relation to this particular legislation under any government that happened to be in power during the time the legislation was on the statute books. The governor in council has the power "of directing, prohibiting, controlling, regulating, determining the course of action this board shall take with respect to any matter that comes within its jurisdiction."
He goes on:
In other words, the responsible government of the country, in its judgment and the exercise of its discretion, has power to control completely the operations of the board.
That was the position of the Prime Minister of the day, speaking on the third reading of the bill, after it had come back, of course, from the committee. He went on to say at page 4273:
I did not conceive it to be the duty of men to take their own fixed opinions with respect to a matter of this kind-
He is speaking of the men who were on the committee.
-but it was their duty, having called witnesses representing every phase of the situation, to listen to what they said, and out of the mass of testimony it became abundantly clear that one group contended they should have an opportunity to show the usefulness of their facilities and that their policies and their programs, based upon those policies, should have an opportunity of being again tried, free from any hampering control, as they contended, such as that of the Producers Limited.
That was the first contention.
That is accorded to them in this bill, but it still holds over their heads the idea that the original provisions of the bill have not been taken from it, but are to be utilized if, as and when in the interests of the producers of this country and of the nation generally it is found desirable to exercise the powers conferred by those provisions.
That is, the powers conferred which have just been read by the minister. He goes further; he says:
That is one side of the matter. Then the other side was that those who represented cooperative and individual marketing were of opinion that a fixed price was essential and desirable. Some of them urged that the factors indicating how that fixed price was to be determined should be stated in the bill.
And we are again discussing that matter over again, as to whether the price should be fixed and stated in the bill. But at that time, may I point out, some of those who were advocating the cooperative marketing of grain in western Canada and elsewhere were advocating a fixed price in the bill rather than the methods which have been followed since. Then he says:
I am free to say that I urged as strongly as I have done to-night that that should not be done for reasons I shall not now traverse.
That is, the Prime Minister of that time thought that, instead of having a set price in the bill, as was urged by some of those who were representatives of cooperative organizations, there should be the method set up which was finally set up in the bill, under which the matter was determined by a board.
We have this bill which the committee accepted for the purpose of doing two things: one, taking care of the surplus accumulations of the wheat of this country. . . .
Canadian Wheat Board

I have already, at an earlier time, placed that paragraph on Hansard. To come now directly to the point which was raised a few moments ago by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar:
Some people think there is objection on the part of importers to buying from one agency. To do so simplifies their business. Although I was not a witness, I endeavoured to ascertain from personal inquiry, and the objection was, as I tried to explain to the committee, that there was an endeavour to sell wheat without regard to the old established agencies. Anyone who knows something of, shall I say, the strength of vested interests who discharge great obligations in marketing, whether it be tea or sugar, wheat or other grains, in the markets of the old country, where the price charged per unit is very small, will understand what the result is if an effort is made to establish, shall I say, a new agency in competition with those old established institutions. My primary reason in rising to-night was to have it known I trust by the inaccurate correspondent of the newspaper-and let him be accurate for once-that as long as this government exists, there is no intention that this country should offer its surplus of grain at fire sale prices or throw its surplus on the markets of the world. I am bound to say in fairness to the committee that this legislation, which is not based on any such idea, was unanimously agreed to by that committee, so that the views which I express are those of the committee unanimously, there being no difference with respect to that whatever.
What I wish to point out is that, in making the last speech which was made-and this is very close to the end of the last speech- the then Prime Minister pointed out clearly that the intention was to use the board which was set up under this act, first to sell the accumulated surplus, next to market the grain of the year 1935 into which we were then going, and so to market the surplus as not to interfere unduly with the marketing of the grain of 1935. Then he goes on to say that the intention of the bill was to leave it open so that the facilities which had 'been set up for the handling of grain in the past could be given another trial in the handling of grain in Canada, and that the facilities used by way of agencies for the selling of the grain in the British market should be used to the fullest extent in connection with the marketing of the grain.
I think all that should be placed on Hansard at this time, during this discussion, in order to make perfectly clear the intention of the government of the day, and I believe that intention has been fairly well carried out by the government which has been in power from that time down to the present.

speechtext: Just before six o'clock the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that certain remarks which had been made by hon. members in this corner of the house could be interpreted as tending to disrupt the good relations which exist between eastern and western Canada. We do not want, by any statements we may make, to endanger confederation. But surely it is not endangering the unity of Canada to suggest to the government that the trade, tariff and monetary policies which they pursue are inimical to the interests of western Canada. Yes, legalized robbery. Let me give the minister an illustration. Millions of dollars' worth of farm machinery have been sold in western Canada by the large manufacturing plants of eastern Canada. That machinery was sold at high prices under a protective tariff. Now that, for a number of reasons, farmers have been unable to pay

Canadian Wheat Board
for that machinery, their overdue accounts are carrying a rate of interest of 10 per cent. That has worked tremendous hardship upon countless numbers of farmers in western Canada, a large percentage of the farmers being in arrears on their machinery and so obliged to pay 10 per cent. We feel that this is an absolute injustice.
Again, the rates of interest which have been charged in western Canada for loans for similar purposes to loans made to farmers in eastern Canada have been anywhere from one to three per cent more than is demanded of the same type of borrowers in eastern Canada. I do not think we should be charged with an endeavour to create disunity or an attempt to destroy or endanger confederation because we suggest that such things are unjust.

If the hon. member says
now that he did not mean what he said in the first instance I am quite willing to forget it and I hope the committee will. I simply want to make this statement. I do not think any member of the house, whether representing the east or the west, can say correctly that the people of eastern Canada, Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces-and that includes myself

have not had every sympathy with the people of the west. And that sympathy has been expressed in the most practical way. If my hon. friends will recognize that, we can agree to differ as to whether they are bearing too great a share of the tariff, and I will not enter into a discussion of that question. I might, say, however, that if I wanted to indulge in recrimination I could strike a balance, have a sort of ledger account showing that the west is receiving this and giving that, and so on. But that would be quite purposeless and useless, and it would only tend to cause disruption among us. In my estimation, I could make a good case as to whether that balance is on the side of the east or the west, but I will not try to do that because that sort of thing only makes for disruption and disunity. I suggest, therefore, that my hon. friends drop that line of argument. If I may say so, they have certainly advanced their case, so far as the tariff is concerned, with such regularity, persistence and repetition that it has become monotonous. I can assure them that we know their point of view thoroughly. If we did not, it certainly would not be for want of having it stated over and over again. I suggest, therefore, now that we understand each other, we might as well go on with the business before the committee and attend to this particular clause, which deals with the limitation of the delivery of wheat to 5,000 bushels by one producer. I think we are entirely out of order in continuing the other discussion.

The second reason is that Canada is the only country that sells wheat to Great Britain on the certificate basis and that means, to those who know the grain business, that Canada grades her wheat, No. 1 hard, No. 1 northern, No. 2 northern, No. 3 northern, No. 4 northern, No. 5 and No. 6 wheat and feed wheat, and other derivatives of the grades in regard to damage done by weather conditions. Other countries sell their wheat on what is known as f.a.q. or fair average quality at the point of shipment. In other words, all the grain that comes into a port is mixed up together and sold as fair average quality on European or British markets. If the Canadian grain were sold as f.a.q., it would mean that all the wheat that came into Fort William would be mixed together and go out as one grade of wheat. In other words, in practice every year we would reach the average of No. 3 northern for our wheat. Argentine wheat is not quite equal to Canadian No. 3 northern in quality. In fact, it generally runs about three cents a bushel below Canadian No. 3 northern. Canadian No. 3 northern generally runs nine cents a bushel below No. 1 northern; or in other words, there is an ordinary preference of nine cents a bushel for No. 1 Canadian northern above an f.a.q. of Canadian wheat. But the price of f.a.q. of Argentine wheat is three cents below that. Therefore, there is an ordinary differential between Canadian No. 1 northern and Argentine wheat of twelve cents a bushel. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the discussion by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has been quite out of order on this section, but if I may be permitted to do so I should like to deal with two points that he raised.
Canadian Wheat Board

He has made a great deal of play over what the policy of the government was with respect to selling wheat.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Do you know?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
No, and my hon. friend does not know either. I challenge the hon. member for Qu'Appelle to point to any section of the Canadian Grain Board Act of 1935 that lays any obligation on the Minister of Trade and Commerce to determine the selling policy of the board with respect to wheat. The act specifically instructs the board that it shall offer wheat continuously for sale, and that it shall use the ordinary channels of trade for the disposal of its wheat, but if in the judgment of the board -not in the judgment of the minister or of the government-the ordinary channels for the disposal of wheat are not sufficient to meet the situation, it may take other steps. But the act specifically lays on the board the duty of conducting the sale of the wheat and the conduct of the whole wheat marketing operations. Nowhere in the act is the obligation laid upon the government or upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce or any other member of the government to direct the selling policy of the board. My hon. friend may be indulging in a bit of political pyrotechnics that may be useful out on the prairies, but as a practical criticism his argument is futile.
He makes great play of another point. He chides the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government for not giving him certain information. He says: "You get weekly reports and we are entitled to be given that information in the house." I wonder if my hon. friend is really serious in that suggestion.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: I certainly am.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Then I must deal with it. The establishment of the wheat board in 1935 was a new departure in the marketing of wheat. It brought the government into a relationship with the business of marketing wheat, and under the act that business is to be conducted by the board. It is most necessary that the board should not disclose its operations to the public. If I may modestly say so, I know a little bit about the marketing of wheat, and there are those not only in this country but in every importing country in the world who would be glad to have the information which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle says the Minister of Trade and Commerce should divulge to this committee. There are many people who would like to know how much wheat the board
[Mr. Crerar.3
has taken delivery from the farmers this year. There are a great many dealers in grain throughout the world who would like to know how much of that wheat has been sold, and how much is still in the hands of the board. But if we were to conduct this business in that way, may I say to my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation who are looking forward to the day when there will be a great deal more government control than there is now, if the business operations entrusted to commissions and boards such as the wheat board were to be disclosed to the public every twenty-dour hours it would make the conduct of such business an impossibility. It would be quite proper, after the whole transactions have been completed, to have information given annually as to the operations of the board, but to disclose now to the public how many million bushels of wheat the board has in its possession would be most unfortunate and would definitely handicap the board in its operations. There can, in my judgment, be no gainsaying that.
I have been in the grain export business for a great many years, if I may be pardoned a personal reference, and as a grain exporter I would have given a great deal at certain times to know what my competitors had sold and how much of their sales they had covered. But that information was never disclosed by private firms. Why then should the government agency, operating in much the same way, disclose information which would be welcomed in every grain importing country in the world. It would place a great handicap on the board and would be unfair to the interests of this country, because I can easily conceive how the disclosure of such information might add to the loss which the wheat board may suffer through its operations this year, and no good interest could possibly be served by it.
May I say further that the opposition in this house between the years 1930 and 1935 asked for the same information. I was not in the house at the time, but I recall reading reports in the newspapers that the opposition had asked for this information. Naturally,
I suppose, they wanted to embarrass the government if they could, but in my judgment the government of the day between 1930 and 1935 were wholly justified in refusing the information.

in the matter of administration. The Minister of Agriculture, who is familiar with these matters, may be able to give a fuller explanation.

speechtext: The difficulty which I see in doing what is suggested is this, that each individual delivers his grain to the board in exactly the same way as he previously delivered it to the wheat pools when the wheat pools were in operation. All the wheat then becomes pooled wheat, and if it is all sold above 70 cents you must pay to the individuals their proportion of that amount which is above 70 cents. So, if you take delivery from an individual of 5,000 bushels at 70 cents and throw that wheat in the pool, and take delivery of another 5,000 bushels at 75 cents, let us say, and throw that in the pool, you find yourself in a position where it is impossible to keep records and finally to pay out from a pool of that kind in the way which is intended under the act.

I said yes. In saying that, I did not mean that they did anything different from what everyone else did at that time. Everyone in Canada who had anything to do with wheat in that period refused to sell at that time even at $1.50 a bushel. They were advised at that time by some of the biggest financial men in Canada that in their opinion wheat was worth more than $1.50 a bushel. I have heard the statement made by people throughout Canada that the pools did not refuse to sell wheat in

1928-29 and 1929-30, but they along with everyone else did refuse to sell wheat at that price at that time.
In this country wheat has been sold through the Winnipeg grain exchange for many years. The wheat pools sold their wheat through the Winnipeg grain exchange; the wheat board has sold its wheat through the Winnipeg grain exchange, and in all the time the pools were in operation they had their salesmen on the floor of the Winnipeg grain exchange. Wheat is sold on that exchange as an auction market-not only option but auction. In other words, buyers bid for wheat and those who have it to sell offer it for sale in the pit. So long as wheat is offered at a stated price, it can never rise above that price. It is only when wheat cannot be bought at a stated price that the price starts to rise; buyers bid higher to get it, the same as in any other auction. In 1928-29 at the end of the crop year, on July 13, 1929, the price of wheat rose to $1,551 a bushel for No. 1 northern. On that day everyone on the Winnipeg grain exchange had refused to sell wheat at $1.50, otherwise the price would never have gone to $1.55, it could not have reached $1.51 so long as anyone was willing to sell at $1.50. The pools had their salesmen there, and every other grain organization in Canada had salesmen there to sell wheat if anyone wanted to sell it. But they all refused to sell wheat at that figure on that day.
Throughout the rest of the month of July, 1929, wheat ranged from $1.55$ No. 1 northern I ort William to $1.78$. But it never got down to $1.50 again. So that during the rest of that month wheat was never offered at $1.50 a bushel.
In August, 1929, the first month of the new crop year, 1929-30, wheat was offered at $1.73$. That was the price. During the mojith of August it ranged from a high of $1.73| to S1.51J, so that throughout the whole month of August wheat was never offered for S1.50 a bushel. During September, until the 16th day of that month, wheat ranged from S1.52J to $1.57$, and then down to $1.50. In other words, from the middle of July wheat was not offered at $1.50 on the Winnipeg grain exchange until September 16. These figures are taken from the Canadian Grain Trade Year Book for 1928-29 and 1929-30. This gives all the statistics in regard to Canadian grain, covering the prices of cash wheat and of options for every day during that period.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Was much wheat moved during the period my hon. friend is reviewing?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Yes, a great deal. As a matter of fact, at that time the cash wheat ran considerably over the options; in other words, there was a high premium for cash wheat. The bidding for cash wheat was strong. I have quoted the cash wheat figures, and cash wheat was selling at a high premium at that time, proving that it was hard to get. During all that period no one in Canada offered to sell wheat at $1.50 a bushel. When anyone, anywhere in this country, says there was no refusal to sell wheat at $1.50, I think he had better look up the records, because no one could have offered wheat at $1.50 a bushel on the Winnipeg grain exchange during that time without that wheat being sold. The market could not have gone higher than $1.50 so long as anyone in this country was willing to sell wheat at that figure. For years we in the west have been hearing that this or that company did not refuse to sell wheat at that figure at that time. I make the definite statement that for sixty days in 1929 everybody refused.

My hon. friend is speaking of options and I am talking about cash wheat. It will be remembered that the 1928 wheat crop was the largest we ever had in Canada, and on August 1, 1930, when we went into the 1929-30 crop year, we were carrying the biggest surplus of wheat we had carried for many years, amounting to 131,000,000 bushels. At that time there was a visible supply, between Canada and the United States, of 377,000,000 in 1928-29 and some
406,000,000 bushels for export in 1929-30. Yet at that time we in this country were foolish enough to refuse to sell that wheat at what we have since found out would have been a very good price. I am not blaming anyone for that; at that time we were all of the same opinion, but I do say we-and I include the wheat pool and anybody else- had better stop telling the people of this country that Canada did not refuse to sell her wheat at that time.

To show the hon. gentleman that he may not be right in his sweeping statement that there was nothing in the 6 cent preference on wheat, let me quote from another authority; authorities differ, of course-assuming my hon. friend to be one. From the United States press release dealing with the trade treaty I quote this paragraph relating to the 6 cent preference on wheat that we had in the British market:
Wheat-The granting of duty-free treatment for wheat by the United Kingdom should prove of marked value to American growers and the American wheat export trade. The import duty on non-empire wheat has been at the rate of 2 shillings per 480 pounds since November 17, 1932.
That is the 6 cent preference. It goes on:
A duty of this size (about six cents per bushel) applicable to wheat from some countries and not others often is sufficient to divert the trade.	.
The concession of free entry for American wheat should benefit also the American transportation and port business.
Now I jump to the bottom paragraph:
The United Kingdom is the leading wheat-import market of the world. Formerly about a fourth of the total American wheat exports were regularly shipped to the United Kingdom. Under the influence of the world economic depression and the establishment of an import duty in 1932-
That is the 6 cent preference:

(with empire wheat remaining duty-free) imports of American wheat into the United Kingdom dropped from 39,267,000 bushels in 1930 to only 9,000 bushels in 1933, while imports from empire sources for the corresponding years rose from 79,234,000 bushels to 140,459,000 bushels.
I do not need to go any further. There are a great many other statements dealing with the matter, but this is good enough authority for me. It may be exaggerated; I do not know. But when my hon. friend says that the right hon. gentleman who preceded me never referred to it, I remember him many times in his most oratorical tones, referring to the foreign ship going over to Great Britain with wheat, and the British ship going over with a cargo of wheat and enjoying the preference in the British market, emphasizing what a great advantage this was to us. But speaking of wheat, here is a page I might read from a report of the Searle Grain Company. These reports are read in this house over and over again, and it is a great advertisement for the company. I am a member of the wheat pool and have been since its inception. I have sold wheat to the pool, but in 1929 I was absolutely against the pool's policy of holding wheat. Why? And why do I object now to reading these wheat pool pamphlets? Because I was opposed to their policies then, and what happened? Wheat is a national commodity, and with the brokers in Winnipeg selling against futures in opposition to the wheat pool's holding policy, the wheat pool could not stand up against it.
There are many places in the world where wheat is sold-Chicago, Winnipeg, London, Liverpool. You can go to Antwerp and Berlin. This is an international commodity and unless you study it as such you will never understand it. A merely provincial or even a dominion policy is entirely too limited. I believe that under section 2 it should be the policy of the wheat board to sell wheat. What happened in Chicago in 1929. Millions of bushels of wheat were sold on the futures market by Russia. Russia was willing to dump wheat in London, and did dump a good deal there. She mechanized her farms and increased her production at the expense of the farmers of the United States and of the Canadian west. I am one of the sufferers from the very policy which some of these people are advocating to-day. If I had not had my wheat in the wheat pool I might have been quite well off to-day. I am not running down the wheat pools, but I am criticizing the policy they adopted in 1929, as I would criticize it if it were followed by any other group. They will not listen to individuals. They will listen only to groups of people. They were unwilling to look at the international situation as a whole.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has spoken of Roumania. AVhat happened. I speak from memory, but my recollection is that Doctor Helmuth Wohlthat, German trade commissioner, entered Roumania last February and started a series of commercial agreements at Bucharest with the Roumanian
Canadian Wheat Board

government. As a result, a general German-Roumanian treaty was signed which gave Germany control of a certain amount of Roumanian wheat. I know, of course, that they are also given control of large quantities of oil. Germany needs oil and wheat. The other day I spoke upon this subject, although briefly, because I did not wish to hold up the business of the house. But let me say that to-day's processes of international trade are far more important than these petty things which happen between one province and another. In the world to-day we are confronted with realities, and unless we face them "we are sunk." Talk about being politically bankrupt-maybe we shall have to have a Hitler in Canada to lead us out of the morass. I know that some of our communist friends say we should have a Stalin. I have no faith in either of these gentlemen. I am in favour of a certain amount of economic nationalism, because I realize its prevalence in the world to-day. Upon what is Roumania's treaty with Germany based? It is written in the treaty that there must be mutual respect as the first condition of friendship; that is a way of getting into Roumania on the part of the German reich. They will take wheat from Roumania; for Germany's deliberate intention is to de-industrialize Roumania in order that it may become a country of peasants, producing wheat and other raw commodities for the Germans, who will be the industrialists. Also they are very much interested in the Dobruja province, which is next door to Bulgaria. I do not need to go further into this international situation. I have studied it a great deal. I have in my constituency more people from more nations of the earth than has probably any other hon. member. I receive letters from these people, who in turn get letters from their homes, and I have some knowledge about the internal situation of their countries.
In conclusion, let me say that to go back to 1929 and to illustrate certain methods by pamphlets which were produced by certain people, and read those pamphlets into Hansard, seems to me foolish. It would be more helpful to go to the Chicago grain exchange and find out who sold wheat short there and on other markets. It is not the Canadian people who did it. We were ruined by an international cartel of traders, but we were not wise enough to see what was going on. The same spirit is abroad in the world to-day, while we sit here carping about petty politics.

I wish to say just a few words with regard to the question of withholding wheat from the market in 1928, 1929

and 1930. It happened to be my duty in 1930, when I attended the imperial conference in London, to straighten out or attempt to straighten out some of the difficulties which resulted from that policy of Canadian wheat marketing. I am not going to lay the blame upon the pools or upon any companies, I am going to say that the policy was a policy of Canadian wheat marketing. What happened was that there was an impression on the great British market that Canadians were deliberately holding back their wheat. Not only in Great Britain, but in Switzerland, Belgium, Holland and other European countries, large milling companies changed the screens on their mills and altered their milling methods so that they could use the' softer wheats from other countries. I remember meeting officially the members of the Baltic exchange in London, and the Liverpool exchange, and discussing the whole matter.
Hon. members will recall that the pools sent to the old country a salesman named Mr. Smith, whose first name I have forgotten. He resided in the old country, and an attempt was made to, shall I say, shortcut the British wheat merchandising organization. This was greatly resented over there. Reference is made in the Turgeon report to Sir Herbert Robson. Sir Herbert, who, I believe, died about a year ago, was one of the greatest advocates of Canadian wheat, and did his utmost to straighten out the difficulty between Canadian wheat marketing organizations and the British buying organizations. It was abundantly clear, however, that there was resentment in the British market and on the continental markets against the attitude which Canadian organizations had assumed. That attitude, furthermore, had much to do with the introduction of a bonus on wheat in Great Britain. It will be recalled that prior to that time the annual production of wheat in Great Britain was only from twenty to twenty-five million bushels. Since then the production has increased. I have not last year's figures, but I believe the amount is now between fifty and fifty-five million bushels, which to that extent represents a smaller market in Great Britain for our wheat.
What to my mind is really more important is the change in the milling processes and methods on the continent. Once they turn to Argentine, Australian and other non-Canadian wheats they are very slow to come back to the hard wheats of Canada. There is no doubt in my mind that we were most unfortunate in the policy of the day. It had very serious results. It is questionable whether there is any advantage in hashing this over

Canadian Wheat Board
again, except for one thing, that we should be careful to avoid in future any such error as we made at that time.
It will be recalled also by those who were associated with the pool that, shortly after the adjustments we were able to make in 1930 were achieved, the pool salesman was recalled from Great Britain and marketing returned to its normal sources.
Let me say, in conclusion, just one thing which I think is of paramount importance when we are discussing the export marketing of Canadian wheat. I believe it is most unwise to attempt to market wheat in Great Britain other than through the established agencies, and in accordance with the methods, practices and customs of that country. That is not because our different ideas of marketing may be wrong, but the point is that existing agencies in Great Britain perform an excellent service; they are well established; their fees and other charges to the British people have been reduced to a moderate and reasonable basis, and they are wedded to well established practices in connection with the handling of this trade. That applies not only to wheat but to all commodities. Any one who knows British methods is aware that no country in the world has a wider and more efficient system of merchandising than has Great Britain. And so what I say is this: We, as Canadians, made a blunder in that period from 1928 to 1930, and at least we should learn from our knowledge and experience of that time to avoid a repetition of those mistakes.

Then I would turn round and sell it to the board. You have the loophole there, and I think it is very important. I have the amendment prepared if you want it.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 6-Application to wheat produced in the eastern division.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: In order to remove any misconception there may be as to the intention of the government that this legislation shall apply to eastern Canada, my colleague will move an amendment:

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
I move to:
Strike out section 14 and substitute the following therefor:
"14. The provisions of this act shall apply mutatis mutandis to wheat produced in the eastern division and the sums certain to be paid producers delivering such wheat shall be fixed by the board with the approval of the governor in council so that they shall bear the same relationship to the sums certain payable in the case of wheat produced in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia as the price of wheat produced in the eastern division bears to the price of wheat in store at Fort William."
Amendment agreed to.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: If this bill is carried, when will it come into effect?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Immediately.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: That leads mie to another question. If it comes into effect immediately, those farmers with wheat on hand will be penalized.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Perhaps I might correct that and say that it will not come into effect until the end of the present crop year.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: That is what I wanted to know.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: The present crop year is on the basis of 80 cents.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Does the amendment just agreed to, make the 70 cent rate applicable to Ontario wheat on exactly the same basis as it applies to the west?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Exactly.
[Mr. Robichaud.l

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: That is clear?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Yes.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported.
